title: What Actually Makes a Proton a Proton?
hook: Textbooks say a proton's identity lives in its three quarks. RHIC data hint it is really carried by a Y-shaped junction of the gluons tying them together.
key_points: Baryon number is the conserved quantity that counts protons and neutrons — its conservation is why protons appear to be stable.
The textbook picture assigns 1/3 of a baryon number to each of the proton's three valence quarks.
Collision data from RHIC instead favour a 'gluon junction': the Y-shaped knot where the three gluon strings meet.
The distinction shows up in how baryon number moves in high-energy collisions — the junction can be transported even when the original quarks are not.
If it holds up, the picture changes how physicists think about matter's stability and about baryon transport in heavy-ion collisions.
content_html: Ask a textbook what makes a proton a proton and you get a simple answer: three quarks, each carrying one-third of a unit of baryon number. Because that number is conserved, a proton has nothing lighter to turn into — which is the deep reason ordinary matter does not simply evaporate.
extra_html:
New analysis of collisions at Brookhaven's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider points somewhere else. The quarks inside a proton are bound by gluon strings that meet in a Y-shaped knot, and the data suggest it is that junction — not the quarks — that carries the baryon number. The two pictures make different predictions about baryon transport: how much of the incoming particles' baryon number ends up in the middle of a collision, far from where the original quarks went. The measurements favour the junction.

It is a striking revision of a decades-old piece of bookkeeping, and if confirmed it reshapes how physicists model baryon flow in heavy-ion collisions and how they think about the origin of matter's stability. As always with a single experiment overturning a textbook picture, the result wants independent confirmation before the textbooks get rewritten. See ScienceDaily's report for the collaboration's framing.

related.title: Measuring the force that traps a quark inside the proton
related.hook: Nobody has ever seen a free quark. A sharpened reconstruction of the actual force tugging on one inside the proton comes out looking like a string pulled at constant tension.

flashcards.prompt: What is baryon number, and why do physicists care that it is conserved?
flashcards.back_html: It is the quantity that counts baryons — protons and neutrons. Because nothing observed so far changes it, a proton has nothing lighter to decay into, which is why ordinary matter is stable.

flashcards.prompt: What does the RHIC result suggest actually carries a proton's baryon number?

choices.text: A Y-shaped junction of the gluon strings connecting the quarks
The three valence quarks, one-third each, as textbooks say
The cloud of virtual quark–antiquark pairs inside the proton

flashcards.explanation_html: The data favour the gluon junction — the knot where the three colour strings meet — rather than the quarks themselves, challenging the standard one-third-per-quark bookkeeping.

flashcards.prompt: Why does it matter experimentally whether quarks or a gluon junction carry baryon number?
flashcards.back_html: The two pictures predict different baryon transport in high-energy collisions: a junction can be dragged into the collision debris even when the original valence quarks are not, changing where baryon number ends up.
